milestone: MSCA-DN assessment framework, ticket R01 of plans/pe08_review_and_pe09_handoff_tickets.md: preserve fidelity declarations during regeneration, before the R04 declaration drafts are prepared
authority: CLAUDE.md §9.1 (docs/ is the durable record), §9.5 (outputs reproducible from documented inputs), §12.1 (an output names its inputs), §12.2 (the status vocabulary), §12.4 (a missing mandatory input is a gate failure, not a papered-over completion), §13.5 (no decision held only in agent memory), §15 (explicit failure over fabricated completion); spec decision 9 (the register's two halves and the two independent fields per sub-section) and decision 18 (the provenance header).

problem.basis: read in the code at 015d9c0 and recorded in the 'not_done' field of msca-dn-line-ending-bindings_2026-10-07
problem.statement: The register's declared half had no durable home, so an operator declaration could not survive an authoring run.
detail: tools/author_msca_dn_workspace.render_register hard-coded declared.sub_sections as an empty list.
tools/import_external_proposal.render_all rewrites both registers through that same renderer, so the importer overwrote the declared half as well.
A declaration typed into a register would therefore be erased by the next run of either tool, and would have failed both byte-equal --check commands in the meantime.

decision.basis: the implementation in tools/fidelity_declarations.py and the verification below
decision.ownership_boundary: The tools own every measured and derived field of the register: the provenance header's hashes, page counts and version markers, the whole derived half, and the revision re-checks. The operator owns declared.sub_sections and nothing else. The tools carry those rows through unchanged: no field is added to a row, none is renamed, none is interpreted and no status is upgraded. The only thing imposed is the row order, taken from the derived inventory so the rendering is canonical whatever order the operator typed.
decision.mechanism: A durable declaration input, one file per revision, at docs/tier3_project_instantiation/source_materials/msca_dn/declarations/<revision_id>.json, holding record_type 'fidelity_declarations', the revision_id, and a sub_sections table. The tools read it and never write it. The register records the input's path and sha256 under declared.declaration_input, so a later edit to the input shows up as a stale register.
decision.why_not_read_back_from_the_register: The other admissible option in R01 was to read the declared half back out of the register and re-emit it. Rejected: the artifact would then be its own source, a rebuild after a deletion would lose every declaration, and §9.5 reproducibility from documented inputs would not hold. With the input file the register is reproducible from the PDF plus that file, and the missing-file rebuild is tested.
decision.missing_input: No file for a revision means no declarations. The register then renders the same empty declared half it carried before this change, byte for byte, including the key order: the declaration_input block appears only when an input exists. Both committed registers are unchanged, so the comparison artifacts that recorded their hashes stay replayable. An empty sub_sections list in a present file is equally valid and is not malformed.
decision.revision_specificity: The file name and the body's revision_id must agree, and each revision reads only its own file. One revision's declarations can never reach another revision's register, because each register renders from its own input. The first revision's declarations are never copied into the superseding revision.
decision.fail_closed: A present-but-malformed input is refused by name and nothing is written: invalid JSON, a wrong record_type, a revision_id that disagrees with the file name, a missing or non-list sub_sections, a row that is not an object, a blank sub_section_id, a missing or empty presence or transformation, a sub-section declared twice, or a sub-section absent from that revision's derived inventory. Invalid data is never silently replaced with an empty list. Both tools read every revision's input before their first write, so a refusal leaves every file as it was.
decision.guard_against_silent_loss: The tools render the register in full, so a sub-section the register declares and the input does not would vanish on the next write. Two acts produce that state, and the input sha256 the register records under declared.declaration_input tells them apart. A withdrawal — the operator removed the row from the input — leaves the register recording older input bytes than the input now has, so the input is the newer statement and the write proceeds. Typing into the output, beside the input the register was rendered from or with no input at all, is refused, naming the rows and the input to move them to. Withdrawing every declaration is an input holding an empty table, never a deleted input: a deleted input cannot be told from a lost one. A sub-section the input does declare may differ freely from the register's copy, since the input owns it and the register is only stale.
decision.format_change: Additive, and only when an input exists: the declared half gains a declaration_input block naming the input's path, sha256, revision and row count. With no input the half keeps its keys and their order, so both committed registers are byte-identical and no recorded hash was regenerated. Nothing in the half is renamed or removed.
decision.check_stays_read_only_and_may_refuse: Both tools run the guard before their first write and the renderer runs it again at each register, so --check can exit 1 with 'refused:' rather than a staleness list. It writes nothing either way. A refusal is the more useful answer at that point: it says where the declarations belong, which a staleness entry does not.
decision.what_the_field_contract_does_not_require: A row needs a sub_section_id in the revision's derived inventory and both fields stating something. A basis and a declared_status are not required, unlike the operator file of runner/working_assumptions.py, which pins both. R01 owns retention; R04 owns what a declaration must say, including the separation of the three fidelity claims and the status each carries. Tightening the contract here would decide R04's format before the operator has. A row with no basis is carried into the register as written and reads there as an unattributed operator statement.
decision.where_the_input_is_documented: In the declared half itself when one exists (declared.declaration_input, with path and sha256), in docs/tier3_project_instantiation/source_materials/msca_dn/declarations/README.md, in harness/HARNESS.md, in both tool docstrings and here. It is deliberately not a row of provenance.inputs: that table is the spec §1 assessment-input table of PDFs, each row carrying a role, a declared version, version markers and a page count, and a JSON declaration file is none of those. With no input there is nothing to name, and the rebuild inputs are then the PDF alone.

consequences.for_r04: The declaration drafts of R04 are authored as declaration inputs under the declarations directory. R04 still owns coverage of a revision's inventory, the separation of the three fidelity claims, and the review status of each row; R01 enforces only the format and the retention. Adopting a draft changes that revision's register bytes, which is the point at which the register's hash in any dependent artifact must be re-recorded.
consequences.for_r05: Both committed registers are unchanged today, so the historical comparison artifacts that recorded fidelity_register.sha256 remain replayable from their documented inputs. A successor comparison run after declarations are adopted reads the new register and must record the new hash.
consequences.for_pe09: The original's import inside the private network declares through the same mechanism: a declarations file for that revision, read by the same tools, with no declaration authored by any tool.
consequences.what_this_does_not_do: It does not validate a declaration's content. Whether a declared presence or transformation is true, and whether the inventory is covered, is operator judgment and remains open; the tools only refuse a malformed or misfiled input.
consequences.residual_risk: A declaration can still be lost in one way: the operator edits the input and, in the same state, has typed a row into the register that the edited input does not declare. The sha256 comparison then reads the input as newer and the typed row is dropped on the next write. --check reports the register as stale before that write, which is the designed signal, but it does not name the row. The mitigation is the documented rule that the register is an output: declarations belong in the input.
